provenance.other: “the foreknowledge of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 1:2; the bare word “foreknowledge” occurs in exactly two, 1 Peter 1:2 and Acts 2:23, where it is coupled to the crucifixion rather than to a calling. “elect according to” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The second half of Alma's sentence has the other half of Peter's chapter: “before the foundation of the world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (John 17:24, Ephesians 1:4, 1 Peter 1:20), and 1 Peter 1:20 is the one that pairs it with foreordination — “foreordained” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reads 'from' where all three read 'before'; the KJV's 'from the foundation of the world' (six verses) is joined to 'prepared' only at Matthew 25:34, 'the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world', which supplies the participle Alma uses three times in five verses.
provenance.significance: Alma 13:3 is the Book of Mormon's fullest statement of foreordination and it is built out of the KJV's fullest one. Recover 1 Peter 1:2's context and the borrowing is doing something the Book of Mormon rarely does: Peter's phrase is the ground of ELECTION — 'Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father' — and Alma takes the whole apparatus of election (called, prepared, from the foundation of the world, foreknowledge) and then, mid-sentence, inserts a clause Peter has no room for: 'in the first place being left to choose good or evil; therefore they having chosen good.' The priests are foreknown because they chose, not chosen because they were foreknown. The verse borrows Calvin's proof-text and reverses its logic inside the sentence, and 13:4-5 spends two more verses insisting that those not called 'were on the same standing with their brethren'. This is metalepsis used against the recalled context rather than in support of it.

13:3.note: 'Being called and prepared from the foundation of the world, according to the foreknowledge of God, on account of their exceeding faith and good works.' Five words reproduce a KJV singleton, and the sentence around them assembles the rest of 1 Peter 1's election vocabulary — prepared, called, from the foundation of the world — with Matthew 25:34 supplying the participle. What makes the row worth more than its word count is what the verse does next: it interposes the free choice of good over evil between the foreknowledge and the calling, which is the one move Peter's sentence forbids. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.
13:3.text: Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied.

provenance.route: Mark 3:5 + Ephesians 4:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “hardness of their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5, and the possessive is the test: Matthew 19:8 has 'hardness of your hearts' and Hebrews 3:8 'harden not your hearts'. “blindness of their” likewise occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:18, where it completes as 'the blindness of their heart'. Alma 13:4 has the first phrase exactly and the second with 'minds' for 'heart' — the noun Paul uses for the same idea at 2 Corinthians 4:4, 'the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not'.
provenance.significance: The two KJV verses that supply this doublet each name a specific refusal, and both are refusals of a manifest sign. Mark 3:5 is the withered hand in the synagogue, where the hardness grieves Jesus in the moment before a healing; Ephesians 4:18 is the alienation of the Gentiles from the life of God. Alma is explaining why some men are not called, and the phrase he reaches for is the one the KJV uses of men who watched a miracle and would not have it. The pairing of a hardened heart with a blinded mind is not itself a KJV collocation: it is assembled here out of two verses that never meet.

13:4.note: 'While others would reject the spirit of God on account of the hardness of their hearts and blindness of their minds.' A KJV singleton reproduced exactly, joined to a second singleton with one noun changed. The phrase is one of the Book of Mormon's standing formulas and this is a new book, so the row is written rather than filed as a repeat (ADJUDICATING §4); the recurrence list carries the earlier adjudications and the two returns inside Alma itself, at 14:6 (the blindness Zeezrom 'had caused among the people') and 14:11 (the hardness of heart that makes the coming judgment just). What the note adds beyond them is the doublet: Mark's hardened heart and Ephesians' blinded understanding are welded into a two-membered formula that neither verse has.
13:4.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.route: Psalm 95:11 → Hebrews 3:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Psalm 95:11 — 'Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into MY rest.'
provenance.other: The mediation is settled by a count and by a pronoun. “enter into his rest” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 3:18, which is the epistle's third-person recasting of the psalm; “into my rest” occurs in exactly four (Psalm 95:11, Hebrews 3:11, Hebrews 4:3, Hebrews 4:5), and every Book of Mormon occurrence in this chapter has 'his'. tools/mediation-check.py reports one decisive point in favour of Psalm 95:11, and that point should be discounted: it is the ABSENCE from Alma of Hebrews' closing clause 'but to them that believed not', and the tool cannot weigh an absence — the same limitation recorded at Jacob 1:7. The pronoun that does decide the case ('my' against 'his') the tool skips as a single common word, by design (ADJUDICATING §4).
provenance.significance: Alma 13 does what Hebrews does and nothing else in the Bible does: it runs the rest of Psalm 95 and the priesthood of Melchizedek through one argument. Hebrews reaches 'enter into his rest' at 3:18-4:11 and Melchizedek at 5:6-7:28, and the joint between them is Hebrews 4:14, 'seeing then that we have a great high priest'. Alma 13 has the same two materials in the same relation — high priests ordained after the order of the Son so that the people 'might enter into his rest' (13:6), the rest entered by those made pure (13:12), the rest urged on the hearers (13:13), Melchizedek in between (13:14-19), and the rest again at the close (13:29). The chapter is not quoting Hebrews so much as reproducing its architecture, and this verse is where the two halves are first bolted together.

13:6.note: 'To teach his commandments unto the children of men, that they also might enter into his rest.' Four words from a KJV singleton, and the singleton is the New Testament's re-pointing of Psalm 95:11 from first person to third. The count decides the mediation against the psalm; the machine's contrary verdict rests on an absence it cannot weigh and is reported here rather than followed. Adjudicated at Jacob 1:7 for that book and written again here because Alma is a new hand and because the phrase is doing new work: in Jacob it carried the wilderness provocation, and here it carries the priesthood, which is Hebrews' own sequence.
13:6.text: And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest, but to them that believed not?

provenance.other: “beginning of days” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “end of life” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse, Hebrews 7:3. The verse's other two singletons are “without father, without mother” and “made like unto the Son of God”. Alma 13:7 has the first phrase exactly and the second with 'years' for 'life'.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 7:3 predicates its four negations of MELCHIZEDEK — the man appears in Genesis without genealogy, and the epistle reads the silence as a likeness to the Son. Alma moves the predicate twice. At 13:7 it belongs to the ORDER ('which order was from the foundation of the world … being without beginning of days or end of years'); at 13:8 to the calling and the ordinance; at 13:9 to the Son himself. So the verse Hebrews uses to make a man resemble the Son is used here to make an institution eternal, and Melchizedek — who does not arrive until 13:14 — is not the subject of it at all. The substitution of 'years' for 'life' follows: an order has years, not a life.

13:7.note: 'Being without beginning of days or end of years, being prepared from eternity to all eternity.' A four-word run from the KJV's densest cluster of singletons, redirected from the man to the priesthood. The chapter will say it twice more, of the ordinance at 13:8 and of the Son at 13:9, which is why the row sits here at first use.
13:7.text: Without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually.

provenance.route: John 1:14 spliced with Hebrews 7:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Both halves are absolute. “the only begotten of the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “full of grace and truth” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse and stand nine words apart in it. Alma 13:9 has them in John's order with Hebrews 7:3's 'without beginning of days' inserted between, and adds one word to the second: 'full of grace, equity and truth'.
provenance.significance: The verse is a splice, and the seam is visible. John 1:14's closing words run 'the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth'; Alma 13:9 runs 'the only begotten of the Father, which is without beginning of days or end of years, which is full of grace, equity and truth'. What has been let into the gap is Hebrews 7:3, so the sentence that identifies the incarnate Word is made to carry the Melchizedek predicate — the two texts this chapter is built from, fused in a single relative chain. The 1830 reading is the more interesting one: 'after the order of the Son OF the only begotten of the Father', which makes the Son and the Only Begotten two persons; 1920 struck the 'of' and restored John's apposition. The first edition shows a borrowing not yet fully assimilated, and the later edition corrected it back toward its source.

13:9.note: 'After the order of the Son of the only begotten of the Father, which is without beginning of days or end of years, which is full of grace, equity and truth.' Six words of a KJV singleton followed, after an interpolation, by five more from the same verse — John 1:14's tail with Hebrews 7:3 spliced into it and 'equity' added to the triad. This is a quotation on the pilot's standard (CONVENTIONS §2) though far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six. The 1830's extra 'of' is recorded in provenance: 1920's deletion moves the text toward the KJV, which is the direction of change CONVENTIONS §8 asks to be flagged.
13:9.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

provenance.other: “made them white in the blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does “washed their robes”, and they are the same verse. Alma 13:11 collapses Revelation's two verbs into one — 'their garments were washed white' — and changes the preposition from 'in' to 'through'.
provenance.significance: Revelation's image is deliberately paradoxical: robes are made WHITE by being washed IN blood. Alma 13:11 keeps the paradox but blunts the mechanism — 'washed white, THROUGH the blood of the Lamb' turns the immersion into an instrument, which is what an English theological idiom does with the figure and what Revelation pointedly does not. The other change is 'robes' to 'garments', which is the Book of Mormon's own word: the formula enters at 1 Nephi 12:11 with 'garments' already in place and keeps it here and at 3 Nephi 27:19. So this row records a formula in its third book with its preposition altered, not a fresh borrowing.

13:11.note: 'They were called after this holy order, and were sanctified, and their garments were washed white, through the blood of the Lamb.' The formula's first adjudication is at 1 Nephi 12:11, where seven words stand verbatim; a new book gets its own row (ADJUDICATING §4). What is new here is the preposition. Revelation 7:14 washes robes IN the blood; Alma 13:11 washes garments white THROUGH it, and the change is in the direction of ordinary devotional English.
13:11.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.other: “sanctified by the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 15:16, where it is said of the offering up of the Gentiles. Alma 13:12 reproduces the five words exactly.
provenance.significance: Paul's clause describes an OFFERING that is sanctified — he is the minister, the Gentiles are the oblation, and the Holy Ghost is what makes the sacrifice acceptable. Alma applies the same five words to men who have been ordained to a priesthood, so the priest of the sentence and its victim change places. Given that 13:11 has just washed their garments in the blood of the Lamb, the sacrificial register of Romans 15:16 is not out of key with the passage; it is the passage's own register.

13:12.note: 'Now they, after being sanctified by the Holy Ghost, having their garments made white, being pure and spotless before God, could not look upon sin, save it were with abhorrence.' Five words from a KJV singleton. Held at moderate rather than high because the phrase is the natural English for the idea and a writer with the KJV's vocabulary could reach it without Romans 15:16 in mind; what argues for the source is that the verse before it has just used a sacrificial image from Revelation, and Romans 15:16 is the KJV's one sanctification-of-an-offering verse.
13:12.whyNot: Five common theological words in their obvious order. The rarity count is real but 'sanctified by the Holy Ghost' is a phrase any nineteenth-century preacher would produce unprompted, and nothing else in Romans 15 is present in Alma 13.
13:12.text: That I should be the minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, ministering the gospel of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “fruits meet for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:8; “meet for repentance” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 3:8 and Acts 26:20, where the noun is 'works' and not 'fruits'. The synoptic control is decisive: Luke 3:8 renders the same saying of John the Baptist as 'Bring forth therefore fruits WORTHY OF repentance'. Alma has Matthew's adjective and Matthew's verb.
provenance.significance: The 1830 spells it 'bring forth fruit METE for repentance' and 1920 changed 'mete' to 'meet'. The direction of that change is the point CONVENTIONS §8 asks to be recorded: the first edition has a homophone that is not the KJV's word, and the later edition corrected it back toward the source. Whoever set the 1830 heard the phrase rather than copied it, which is evidence about the mode of transmission and not merely about spelling. The borrowing is also placed: Matthew 3:8 is John the Baptist at the Jordan, and Alma is at Ammonihah demanding the same of a city that has just refused him.

13:13.note: 'I would that ye should humble yourselves before God, and bring forth fruit mete for repentance, that ye may also enter into that rest.' Four words of a KJV singleton, and the alternative synoptic wording at Luke 3:8 rules Matthew in rather than out. The 1830's 'mete' for 'meet' is recorded above as a transmission datum.
13:13.text: Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:

provenance.route: Psalm 110:4 → Hebrews 5:6, 5:10, 6:20, 7:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Psalm 110:4 — 'Thou art a PRIEST for ever after the order of Melchizedek.'
provenance.other: “an high priest for ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:20; “called of God an high priest” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 5:10; “called of God” occurs in exactly two, Hebrews 5:4 and 5:10, both of them about who may take the office. The single word that decides the mediation is 'high': Psalm 110:4 and its four New Testament citations all read 'after the order of Melchizedek', but only the epistle promotes the priest to a HIGH priest, and Alma 13:14 has 'a High Priest after this same order … took upon him the High Priesthood forever'.
provenance.significance: tools/mediation-check.py run on this verse against Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 6:20 returns divergences pointing BOTH ways, and its warning that this is a real finding rather than a bug is exactly right. The epistle supplies the substance — 'made an high priest for ever' — while the psalm supplies the orthography, because the KJV spells the name 'Melchizedek' in Genesis 14:18 and Psalm 110:4 and 'Melchisedec' in all six of its Hebrews occurrences, and the Book of Mormon's four occurrences (13:14, 13:15, 13:17, 13:18) are all the Old Testament spelling. So the chapter's Melchizedek carries a Hebrew name and a Greek epistle's argument. Where a nineteenth-century writer got the name from an English Bible and the doctrine from Hebrews, that is precisely the split you would expect; where a sixth-century Nephite had brass plates, the Hebrews half has no source at all.

13:14.note: 'Humble yourselves even as the people in the days of Melchizedek, who was also a High Priest after this same order which I have spoken, who also took upon him the High Priesthood forever.' Two KJV singletons stand behind the sentence, and both are in Hebrews rather than in the psalm Hebrews is expounding. The mediation tool's split verdict is the finding and is written up in provenance: substance from the epistle, spelling from the Old Testament.
13:14.text: Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.

provenance.route: Genesis 14:20 → Hebrews 7:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Genesis 14:20 — 'And he gave him TITHES OF ALL.'
provenance.other: “a tenth part of all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 7:2; “tithes of all” occurs in exactly two, Genesis 14:20 and Luke 18:12 (the Pharisee's boast); “gave the tenth” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 7:4. Alma 13:15 has BOTH the Genesis noun and the Hebrews measure: 'Abraham paid tithes … paid tithes of one tenth part of all he possessed.' tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point in favour of Hebrews 7:2 — the Book of Mormon has 'To whom also Abraham', not Genesis's 'And blessed be the most high God … And he'.
provenance.significance: Genesis 14:20 never says who paid whom. Its 'he gave him tithes of all' is famously ambiguous in the Hebrew and in the KJV, and it is Hebrews 7:2 that fixes the direction — 'To whom also ABRAHAM gave a tenth part of all' — because the epistle's whole argument requires Abraham to be the lesser party. Alma 13:15 has the epistle's disambiguation, twice over and emphatically: 'this same Melchizedek to whom Abraham paid tithes; yea, even our father Abraham paid tithes.' A text reading Genesis alone could not be this sure. The verse also over-explains the measure, glossing 'tithes' with 'one tenth part of all', which is Hebrews' phrase used as a definition of the Genesis one — the two verses laid side by side.

13:15.note: 'And it was this same Melchizedek to whom Abraham paid tithes; yea, even our father Abraham paid tithes of one tenth part of all he possessed.' Hardy MSI cross-references Genesis 14:18-20 at this verse, which is right about the episode; the wording is Hebrews'. The measure 'a tenth part of all' is a KJV singleton in Hebrews 7:2, and the direction of payment — Abraham to Melchizedek — is a fact the Genesis verse does not state and the epistle does. Both halves of Alma's doubled clause therefore come through the New Testament. (1830 reads 'one tenth part'; 1920 hyphenated it to 'one-tenth part'.)
13:15.text: To whom also Abraham gave a tenth part of all; first being by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace;

provenance.other: “king of Salem” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Genesis 14:18, Hebrews 7:1 and Hebrews 7:2. tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for Genesis 14:18 over Hebrews 7:1, and the point is the name itself — the Book of Mormon spells 'Melchizedek', which is the KJV's Genesis and Psalm 110 spelling, against Hebrews' 'Melchisedec'. Every one of the Book of Mormon's four occurrences of the name (Alma 13:14, 13:15, 13:17, 13:18) has the Old Testament form.
provenance.significance: This verse is where the chapter's one substantial non-biblical claim sits: that Melchizedek's people 'had waxed strong in iniquity and abominations' and that he preached repentance to them. Neither Genesis 14 nor Hebrews 7 says anything whatever about the people of Salem — Genesis gives Melchizedek four clauses and Hebrews gives him an argument, and in both he is a figure without a congregation. The Book of Mormon supplies him with one, and supplies him with the career of a Nephite prophet: a wicked city, a call to repentance, a repentance granted, peace established. Alma is preaching in Ammonihah, a city that has just cast out Alma himself, and the Melchizedek he offers them is a preacher whose wicked city listened.

13:17.note: 'Now this Melchizedek was a king over the land of Salem.' The title is one of three KJV verses and the spelling settles which: Genesis's 'Melchizedek', not Hebrews' 'Melchisedec'. The mediation is recorded as direct-OT for this row on the strength of the orthography; the row at 13:14 carries the New Testament mediation for the substance, and the two together are the finding rather than either alone. What follows the title in this verse has no biblical source at all, which is noted in provenance because a catalogue of borrowings should say where the borrowing stops.
13:17.text: And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.

provenance.route: Hebrews 7:2's etymological gloss, with Isaiah 9:6 supplying the title → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Prince of Peace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 9:6. Hebrews 7:2's gloss reads 'King of Salem, which is, King of peace'. Alma 13:18 reproduces the gloss's logic and substitutes the Isaiah title for the Hebrews one: 'therefore he was called the Prince of Peace, FOR HE WAS THE KING OF SALEM'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most economical piece of exegesis and it is a substitution. Hebrews 7:2 derives a title from a place-name — Salem is peace, therefore Melchizedek is King of peace — and the derivation is the epistle's, not Genesis's. Alma keeps the derivation intact, including the causal 'for', and puts a different title in the slot: not Hebrews' 'King of peace' but Isaiah 9:6's 'Prince of Peace', which is a KJV singleton and which the Christian reading of Isaiah 9:6 assigns to the Messiah alone. The effect is to make the argument of Hebrews 7 explicit in one word. Hebrews spends a chapter showing Melchizedek to be a type of Christ by resemblances and silences; Alma simply gives him Christ's messianic title and lets the etymology justify it. The Book of Mormon has already used Isaiah 9:6 in full at 2 Nephi 19:6, so the title is in the book's own text before it is applied to a man here.

13:18.note: 'Melchizedek did establish peace in the land in his days; therefore he was called the Prince of Peace, for he was the king of Salem.' No clause is reproduced, which is why this is catalogued as an allusion and not a quotation, but the move is unmistakable: Hebrews 7:2's Salem-means-peace etymology with Isaiah 9:6's messianic title dropped into the place where Hebrews wrote 'King of peace'. The two sources are a KJV singleton and the one epistle that argues Melchizedek's typology, and no other English verse joins a title of peace to the name Salem.
13:18.text: To whom also Abraham gave a tenth part of all; first being by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace;

provenance.other: “consider how great this man was” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 7:4, and it is the KJV's only sentence insisting on Melchizedek's greatness; Hebrews 7:7 restates it as 'the less is blessed of the better'. Alma 13:19 has the claim without the words: 'there were many before him, and also there were many afterwards, but none were greater.' The framing formula — none before or after him was his like — is an Old Testament royal idiom: “none like him” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, among them 2 Kings 18:5 of Hezekiah, 'after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor any that were before him'.
provenance.significance: The sentence is doing two jobs at once. Its content is Hebrews 7:4's — that Melchizedek's greatness is the argument, and that the reader should weigh it — and its shape is the Deuteronomistic historian's verdict on a good king, which the KJV pronounces over Hezekiah and Josiah in almost these words. Melchizedek is a king, and the formula the Book of Mormon uses to rank him is the formula 2 Kings uses to rank kings. The second clause is stranger and worth flagging: 'therefore of him they have more particularly made mention' is a claim about a documentary record, and the record in which Melchizedek is more particularly mentioned is Hebrews 7.

13:19.note: 'Now there were many before him, and also there were many afterwards, but none were greater; therefore of him they have more particularly made mention.' No verbal contact with Hebrews 7:4 beyond the comparative, so this is an echo and is held at moderate. It is written rather than excluded because the claim is peculiar: nothing in Genesis 14 makes Melchizedek great, and the one place in the KJV where his greatness is asserted and made to carry an argument is the chapter Alma 13:14-18 has just been quarrying.
13:19.whyNot: The shared element is a comparative adjective. A writer with no Hebrews at all could say that none was greater, and the 2 Kings formula behind the sentence's shape is common enough that its presence proves nothing about which specific verse is in view.
13:19.text: Now consider how great this man was, unto whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils.

provenance.route: Isaiah 49:8 → 2 Corinthians 6:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Isaiah 49:8 — 'and in A day of salvation have I helped thee', a past-tense report with the indefinite article.
provenance.other: “day of salvation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 49:8 and 2 Corinthians 6:2. tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence, because Alma reproduces neither verse's surrounding clause; the case has to be made from the two words the tool skips. Isaiah has 'in A day of salvation have I helped thee' — indefinite, past, and spoken to the servant; Paul has 'behold, NOW IS THE day of salvation' — definite, present, and addressed to hearers. Alma 13:21 is 'Now is the time to repent, for THE day of salvation draweth nigh': definite article, present urgency, second person. There is also a control the Book of Mormon supplies itself. Isaiah 49:8 stands transcribed in this book at 1 Nephi 21:8, in Isaiah's form, 'in a day of salvation have I helped thee'. The Old Testament wording was available in the Book of Mormon's own text and is not the wording Alma uses.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 6:2 is Paul's one verse of pure temporal urgency — he quotes Isaiah's promise and then twice converts it to the present tense, 'now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation', to make an appeal. Alma 13:21 is doing precisely that and at precisely that pitch: he stretches out his hand, cries with a mighty voice, and says 'Now is the time to repent'. The one adjustment is eschatological. Paul says the day of salvation IS; Alma says it DRAWETH NIGH, because in his chronology the atonement is still future. The borrowing keeps Paul's urgency and moves his tense back by a century.

13:21.note: 'He stretched forth his hand unto them and cried with a mighty voice, saying, Now is the time to repent, for the day of salvation draweth nigh.' One of two KJV verses, and the mediation is decided by the article and the tense rather than by the machine, which finds no shared clause to test. The strongest control is internal: this book transcribes Isaiah 49:8 at 1 Nephi 21:8 with Isaiah's indefinite 'a day of salvation', and Alma has Paul's definite one.
13:21.text: (For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)

provenance.route: Luke 2:10 fused with Luke 1:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “tidings of great joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 2:10, where the angel's adjective is 'good'. “glad tidings” occurs in exactly four (Luke 1:19, Luke 8:1, Acts 13:32, Romans 10:15), and the first of them is Gabriel's — 'am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings'. Alma 13:22 has the two welded: 'glad tidings of great joy', a phrase that is in no KJV verse and is made of two that are.
provenance.significance: Both of the fused phrases are spoken BY AN ANGEL in Luke's first two chapters, and Alma 13:22 is about angels: 'the voice of the Lord, BY THE MOUTH OF ANGELS, doth declare it unto all nations … he doth sound these glad tidings among all his people.' Luke 1:19 is Gabriel to Zacharias, Luke 2:10 is the angel to the shepherds, and Alma has taken a phrase from each to describe what angels are at this moment declaring in his own land. The chapter goes on to complete the annunciation cluster at 13:23 with Luke 1:28's 'highly favoured'. The metalepsis is exact: the Nephites at Ammonihah are put in the position of the people to whom Luke's angels announced a birth, in a chapter whose whole burden is that the birth has not happened yet.

13:22.note: 'That they may have glad tidings of great joy; yea, and he doth sound these glad tidings among all his people.' A phrase that exists in no KJV verse, assembled out of the two angelic-announcement formulas of Luke 1-2. The n-gram stream found Luke 2:10; the second half of the fusion, and the fact that Luke 1:28 lands in the next verse, came from reading the passage.
13:22.text: And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.

provenance.other: “highly favoured” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:28, the angel's salutation to Mary. The 1830 spells it in the American form, 'highly favored', which is the Book of Mormon's orthography throughout and does not weaken the identification.
provenance.significance: Taken alone this would be two words and not worth a row. Taken with the verse before it, it completes a set: Luke 1:19's 'glad tidings' and Luke 2:10's 'tidings of great joy' at 13:22, and Luke 1:28's 'highly favoured' here, all three of them the words of an angel announcing the coming of Christ, and all three inside two verses of a passage about angels declaring his coming. What is said to Mary of her singular election — 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured' — is said by Alma of a whole people: 'therefore we are thus highly favored, for we have these glad tidings declared unto us in all parts of our vineyard.'

13:23.note: 'Therefore we are thus highly favored, for we have these glad tidings declared unto us in all parts of our vineyard.' A KJV singleton of two words, which on its own would be an accident. It is written because of its company: this is the third phrase from Luke's annunciation scenes in two verses, and the third that is spoken by an angel. Held at moderate because the individual contact is slight.
13:23.whyNot: Two words, and 'highly favoured' is ordinary English that a writer need not have got from Luke. The argument is entirely from the cluster at 13:22-23, and if the reader declines the cluster this row falls with it.
13:23.text: And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.

provenance.other: “in a strange land” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Exodus 2:22 and 18:3 (Moses naming Gershom), Psalm 137:4 (the exiles by the rivers of Babylon) and Acts 7:6 (Stephen quoting the promise to Abraham). “wanderers” occurs in exactly two, Jeremiah 48:12 and Hosea 9:17, and neither is in this sense, so the contact is with the second half of the phrase only.
provenance.significance: Of the four candidates, Psalm 137:4 is the one whose situation is Alma's. Lehi's colony left Jerusalem on the eve of the deportation the psalm laments, and the psalm's question — 'How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?' — is exactly the question a Nephite preacher answering it in the affirmative would have to answer: Alma's clause is 'this because of our being wanderers in a strange land; THEREFORE we are thus highly favored', which turns exile into privilege. The Book of Mormon has taken the psalm's premise and reversed its conclusion. Exodus 2:22 and Acts 7:6 remain live alternatives and are recorded as such.

13:23.note: 'And this because of our being wanderers in a strange land.' One of four KJV verses, and the choice among them is an argument from situation rather than from wording, which is why the row is an echo at moderate. Proposed under the generative posture (CONVENTIONS §0a): a text written by exiles from the Jerusalem of 600 BC, reaching for the KJV's exile phrase and inverting the exile psalm's despair, is worth putting on the table even though the four candidate verses cannot be separated on wording alone.
13:23.whyNot: The four KJV verses containing 'in a strange land' cannot be distinguished by anything Alma 13:23 reproduces, and the phrase is common enough English that no source may be in view at all. Nothing else from Psalm 137 appears anywhere near.
13:23.text: How shall we sing the LORD’s song in a strange land?

provenance.other: “which was in them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 1:11 — 'the Spirit of Christ WHICH WAS IN THEM did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ'. “testified beforehand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The noun Alma substitutes is also a singleton: “the spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:10, 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy'. Alma 13:26 has the frame of the first and the noun of the second: 'according to the spirit of prophecy which was in them'.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 1:10-12 is the New Testament's one sustained account of what prophets before Christ knew and how they knew it: they enquired and searched diligently, the Spirit of Christ in them testified beforehand of his sufferings, it was revealed that they ministered not to themselves but to a later generation, and 'which things the angels desire to look into'. Alma 13:24-26 is that paragraph rearranged into a Nephite present: angels are declaring it now, just and holy men will be told by the mouth of angels at the time of his coming, and all of it happens so 'that the words of our fathers might be fulfilled, according to that which they have spoken concerning him, which was according to the spirit of prophecy which was in them'. Peter's prophets are Alma's fathers; Peter's later generation is Alma's congregation; and Peter's angels, who in 1:12 only desire to look into the gospel, have in Alma become the ones who announce it. With 1 Peter 1:2 standing behind 13:3, the chapter opens and closes on the same page of the same epistle.

13:26.note: 'That the words of our fathers might be fulfilled, according to that which they have spoken concerning him, which was according to the spirit of prophecy which was in them.' Four words of a KJV singleton with the singleton's own noun ('the Spirit of Christ') replaced by another singleton's ('the spirit of prophecy', Revelation 19:10). The machine proposed Romans 1:4 here on 'according to the spirit of', which is the right string and the wrong verse; 1 Peter 1:11 supplies the whole clause and the whole situation.
13:26.text: Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 10:13 + Matthew 26:41 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “above that ye are able” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 10:13; “watch and pray” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 26:41 and Mark 13:33. Alma 13:28 has both: 'watch and pray continually, that ye may not be tempted above that which ye can bear.' The verb is the tell. Paul's clause is 'tempted above that ye are ABLE', and 'bear' is his next clause — 'that ye may be able to BEAR it' — so Alma's 'above that which ye can bear' is 1 Corinthians 10:13's opening and closing joined across the middle of the verse. A writer with only the phrase would have written 'able'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 26:41's 'Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation' and 1 Corinthians 10:13's promise about temptation are the KJV's two great temptation texts, and Alma 13:28 makes one sentence of them, replacing Matthew's purpose clause with Paul's. The result is a promise Matthew does not give: Gethsemane's imperative issued with Corinth's guarantee attached. That the verse also folds Paul's escape clause back into its own protasis — 'that ye may not be tempted above that which ye can bear' — shows the whole of 1 Corinthians 10:13 in view rather than a remembered phrase from it. The phrase returns two chapters later, and its return is the sermon's only recorded effect: at Alma 15:17 the converts of Sidom 'began to assemble themselves together at their sanctuaries to worship God before the altar, WATCHING AND PRAYING CONTINUALLY, that they might be delivered from Satan'. The narrator is quoting Alma's own imperative back as a description of obedience, and the purpose clause he supplies for it — deliverance from Satan — is Matthew 26:41's temptation rather than Paul's.

13:28.note: 'Watch and pray continually, that ye may not be tempted above that which ye can bear.' Two of the KJV's most distinctive temptation clauses in one sentence, one of them a singleton. The decisive detail is 'bear' rather than 'able': it is the word from the far end of 1 Corinthians 10:13, which means the source verse was in view whole. 1 Corinthians 10:13 is one of the Book of Mormon's standing sources and its earlier adjudications are listed; the row is written because Alma is a new book and because the fusion with Matthew 26:41 is new here.
13:28.text: There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.

provenance.route: Revelation 21:8 (with 2 Peter 2:4) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “second death” occurs in exactly four KJV verses and all four are in Revelation (2:11, 20:6, 20:14, 21:8); 21:8 is the one that names who suffers it. The other half of Alma's sentence has no KJV verse behind it as it stands — “chains of hell” occurs in no KJV verse — and its nearest source is 2 Peter 2:4's “chains of darkness”, a KJV singleton, where the bound parties are the angels that sinned.
provenance.significance: The pairing is the point. Revelation's second death is the lake of fire at the end of the judgment; 2 Peter's chains of darkness are the reservation of the fallen angels UNTIL that judgment. Alma 13:30 asks that his hearers escape both, and in the right order — not bound down by the chains while they wait, not suffering the second death when they arrive. The Book of Mormon's own substitution, 'hell' for 'darkness', makes the destination explicit where 2 Peter left it as a condition, and the phrase so formed becomes one of the book's standing formulas.

13:30.note: 'That ye may not be bound down by the chains of hell, that ye may not suffer the second death.' Both halves are catalogued: the second death is Revelation's, four verses and no other book, and the chains are 2 Peter 2:4's with one noun changed. Held at moderate because neither phrase is reproduced with more than the words it needs and both had already become Book of Mormon idiom before Alma 13, which is what the recurrence list records.
13:30.text: But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

provenance.other: “which are not written in this book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:30, and so does the shorter “not written in this book”. Alma 13:31 reproduces the six-word relative clause exactly: 'Alma spake many more words unto the people, which are not written in this book.'
provenance.significance: John 20:30 is the KJV's colophon verse — the evangelist stopping and telling the reader that his book is a selection from a larger record — and the Book of Mormon uses it as a colophon too, at the close of a sermon rather than of a gospel. Recover John's context and the borrowed clause carries John 20:31 with it: 'but these are written, that ye might believe.' A formula whose function in its source is to justify a canon's incompleteness is doing the same work here, at the end of the longest doctrinal discourse in the book so far, and the 1830 sets it as the last words of the chapter.

13:31.note: 'And it came to pass that Alma spake many more words unto the people, which are not written in this book.' Six words of a KJV singleton, in order and without change. The formula is adjudicated for Mosiah at 1:8; Alma is a new book and gets its own row (ADJUDICATING §4). 1920 deleted the 1830's opening 'And it came to pass that', which shortens the sentence toward John's but does not touch the borrowed clause.
13:31.text: And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book:
